🔗📁This was a race of reduced numbers, foreshortened at the start to prevent horses arriving at the first fence overexcited. The restricted field of 34 was further reduced to 32 by two non-runners, Chambard and Run Wild Fred, to leave the smallest number of entries for a quarter of a century. And the safety measures seemed to work: this was the first National since 2018 not to precipitate an equine fatality. Indeed there was only one faller: Corach Rambler, last year’s winner and this year’s co-favourite, which hit the turf while loose as it negotiated the second fence, having unseated 2023’s winning jockey Davy Russell at the first.

🔗📁Townend was aboard the other co-favourite. Not that you would have realised that in the early stages. Riding the horse from the Willie Mullins stable, owned by the serial Irish winner JP McManus, Townend bided his time. For much of the first loop of Aintree’s course, the French horse Glengouly led the way. I Am Maximus was tucked in on the inside, keeping his pace in reserve. At the Chair on the first lap he stumbled. “I thought he’d let Paul out over his ears,” said Mullins. “Paul told me afterwards he was only doing enough to get over the fences, and he clipped a couple of others too. It’s probably the way to do Aintree rather than big extravagant jumps that sap energy. But I admit I was worried.”

🔗📁Townend, however, quickly regained control. “He made that mistake at the Chair, which slowed him down,” he explained. “I was anxious not to rush him back in.” And indeed, even as the denouement approached, the horse was still nowhere near the front. He jumped the final fence with five horses ahead of him, then, as he took the Elbow, as the course bends round to the winning straight, he was in third place. That is when the horse applied the afterburners, easing away to a significant victory by seven and a half lengths. “Not too many quicken up at the Elbow and hit the line,” said Townend. “We knew the engine was in there. It was a huge performance.”

🔗📁“He’s only a small, little horse but he has such heart,” Gavin Cromwell said of Raz De Maree, who made him the second trainer to win a Welsh Grand National from Ireland. A farrier by trade, Cromwell has shod Gold Cup and Grand National winners for other people but has now won a major race of his own after a 13-year training career. It was a desire to avoid breaking Raz De Maree’s enormous heart that prompted Cromwell to book James Bowen, believed to be the youngest winning rider in this race’s rich history. With an established jockey, the horse would have had to shoulder more than 11 stone, the kind of burden under which he has struggled in the past. Bowen’s 5lb claim, granted by the rules to compensate for his inexperience, was reckoned by the trainer to be gold dust for a race run on such a stamina-sapping surface.

🔗📁But the value of a talent like Bowen lies not just in his claim and there is no doubt he will still be in great demand when this is wiped out. The great difficulty with a slogger like Raz De Maree is keeping within shouting distance of the rest through the first half of the race and Bowen gave himself every chance by being in the front rank at the off. The pair soon slid gently back through the field but there was no panicking from the young man in the saddle and they started picking off their rivals down the back straight on the final circuit. They were eighth at the turn for home but had hit the front by the second-last.

🔗📁Bowen said: “To win this, first season riding, it’s amazing.” Asked for his earliest memory of the Welsh National, the biggest race in his native country, Bowen reached all the way back to the 2013 running when he led up a 100-1 shot trained by his father, making everyone within earshot feel very old. “It’s massive,” he said. “You grow up watching these races, don’t you? If you’d told me I was going to win the Welsh Grand National a year ago, I’d never have believed you because I was still pony racing then. From the age of eight, I knew I was going to be a jockey.”

🔗📁While a point to point rider last winter, he broke the record for wins in a season by a novice jockey and built up such a reputation that trainers were competing to sign him up through the summer. Nicky Henderson, the reigning champion, eventually won that battle and it allowed him to take some pleasure in this result, even though his own Beware The Bear was pulled up. “At least a little bit of Seven Barrows won,” he said. His father, the trainer Peter Bowen, meanwhile, was almost bursting with pride. “He’s always been very, very competitive,” he said of his youngest son. “I remember the first pony race he rode in when he was nine. He finished third and was devastated. He won’t give in to nothing, trains hard as well. He deserves it.”

🔗📁Two decades have passed since French Holly and Andrew Thornton became the last winners of the Sidney Banks Memorial Hurdle to go on to Grade One success at Cheltenham a month later. Few of the winners since have shown as much natural talent as Vinndication, however, and Kim Bailey’s unbeaten five-year-old is now as short as 14-1 to beat a field including Samcro, the hot favourite, in the Ballymore Novice Hurdle on 14 March. Before his price could represent any value, though, Bailey would need to commit Vinndication to run, which is not, yet, something he is inclined to do. His gelding stayed on strongly to beat Western Ryder by nearly four lengths here and was well on top at the line, but Vinndication’s inexperience remains a concern after only three starts over hurdles.

🔗📁Bailey has depth among his novice hurdlers this season, with both First Flow and Red River running to a high standard in recent weeks. He is in little doubt, though, that Vinndication is the best prospect in his stable. “Red River is the same age [as Vinndication] but he’s a different horse as he’s had a point-to-point run,” Bailey said. “Vinndication has two entries [at the Cheltenham Festival] but I wouldn’t think we’d go three miles [in the Albert Bartlett Novice Hurdle] with him, we’ll leave that one to Red River. “I’ve said for a long time that he’s our best novice, and David [Bass, his jockey] said when he won on him at Ludlow [in November] that he was the best horse of mine that he’d ridden. He’s as hard as nails, and from day one he’s wanted to be good. You get humans who are the same and have a natural ability to be good at what they do, and he’s just one of those.”

🔗📁Fletcher also struck gold with Red Alligator, but it was his wins on Ginger McCain's Red Rum that propelled the jockey into the spotlight RACING MOURNS Grand National winner Brian Fletcher, who rode Red Rum to win the race twice has died, aged 69 BRIAN FLETCHER, who rode three winners of the Grand National including two on Red Rum, has died, aged 69. Fletcher first came to prominence at Aintree when he steered Red Alligator to third place in the famous renewal won by Foinavon in 1967, when just a 19-year-old. He made no mistake the following year on the Denys Smith-trained Red Alligator and went on to become part of Aintree folklore for his wins on Ginger McCain’s Red Rum.

🔗📁The National story of Red Rum began back in 1973 when he caught the gallant Australian chaser Crisp in the final strides of one of the most thrilling finishes in the race’s history. But for Fletcher, the drama began to unfold two fences from the winning post. He saw Crisp flash his tail, and with the confidence born of having already been a National winner with Red Alligator, Fletcher crouched lower in the saddle. Red Rum went on to become the most successful horse ever to race over the daunting Aintree fences, teaming up once more with Fletcher the following year, although Tommy Stack was on board for ‘Rummy’s’ third win in 1977.

🔗📁A glittering career also saw Fletcher win the Scottish National as well as finish runner-up to Josh Gifford in the jockeys’ title race. He retired in 1977. He said some years ago he did not regard either of Red Rum’s victories in the Grand National as the best race of his career, but instead plumped for the Aintree great’s triumph in the Scottish version of 1974. Recalling the worst moment, which was when he lost the ride on Red Rum – “I was devastated,” he said. Former champion jockey Peter Scudamore described Fletcher as an “unsung hero” He told Press Association Sport: “He was an unsung hero and without the unsung heroes of that era National Hunt racing wouldn’t be where it is today.

🔗📁Have finished between 1st and 4th in a steeplechase over 2 miles 7½ furlongs or further. ‌ What is the race distance? The official distance is four miles, two furlongs and 74 yards (4m 2f 74y). This distance is measured two yards inside the innermost rail. The Grand National is the longest jump race held in the UK. ‌ How many fences are there? There are 16 individual fences in the race, 14 of which are jumped twice. That makes a total of 30 jumps. The fences are made from Sitka spruce or Norway spruce, which is transported to Aintree from the Lake District. It takes about three weeks to construct all the fences which include the famous Beecher’s Brook and The Chair.

🔗📁‌ ‌ View 4 Images Major changes have been made to the Grand National (Image: Getty Images) What are the changes to the 2024 Grand National? Significant changes have been made. The alterations have been made after animal rights protesters ambushed the event last year - causing a delay of over 15 minutes. ‌ However, the Jockey Club insists that the changes did not come as a direct response to those protests. The most significant changes are as follows: The field has been reduced from 40 horses to a maximum of 34. The first fence has been brought forward, towards the start line, by 60 yards in order to reduce the speed at which the horses reach it.

🔗📁The start will now be a standing start at the tape, rather than the traditional rolling start. This change is also designed to reduce the speed that horses arrive at the first obstacle. Each horse must have an official rating of at least 130 - rather than 125. Fence 11 has been reduced in height by two inches and will have the drop on the landing side reduced. Horses will no longer be led onto the course by a handler before the race, instead being released to canter in front of the grandstands. The start time has been moved from 5.15pm to 4pm.

🔗📁After having spent so long at the top of the game, it’s little wonder Thornton is opinionated on how the sport has changed for his colleagues. He said: “I’d say the professionalism of the lads now is the biggest change. The advances in physiotherapy, improvement in diet and fitness – you can’t play at this game or you get found out. “I think that was brought about by John Francome. I’ve spanned two eras really, with Francs, Peter Scudamore, Richard Dunwoody and Jamie Osborne passing on to AP (McCoy), Dicky (Richard Johnson) and Timmy Murphy et al. “I don’t think it will be possible for anyone to match the number AP and Dicky have racked up, simply because there is no trainer as dominant these days.”

🔗📁Having received the acclaim of Cheltenham’s cauldron of a winner’s enclosure no fewer than 43 times in his 24-year career, Barry Geraghty seems to have decided that the announcement of his retirement could be a little more low-key. A simple tweet at 11pm on Saturday evening said “a big thank you” to the family, friends and everyone who had supported him, adding: “I’ve been blessed to have had a wonderful career and I’m looking to what the future holds.” Geraghty, by any measure, was one of the finest of all National Hunt jockeys and his announcement means that all three of the outstanding big-race riders who dominated the Cheltenham Festival in the first two decades of the century – Geraghty, Ruby Walsh and Tony McCoy – have now hung up their boots.

🔗📁To no one’s great surprise, the card at Catterick has failed to pass an inspection and the turf cards scheduled for Musselburgh and Market Rasen on Wednesday have also been abandoned. Chelmsford City, however, will race on the all-weather as planned, which means that with Lingfield also getting the go-ahead, racing will defy the Beast with a total of 13 races on Tuesday. Jorvik Dancer (4.15) is probably the pick of the prices in the sprint handicap at Chelmsford City. He completed a swift hat-trick in late December and early January but remains fairly weighted on the pick of his recent form and is a fair bet at around 11-4. Carolinae (3.30) should also go well at Lingfield, but with the Cheltenham Festival now imminent, punters may well spend some time instead looking at the ante-post markets. Willie Mullins, the leading trainer at the Festival in four of the last five seasons, opened his doors to the media on Monday, and here is a round-up of his comments on some of his leading contenders.

🔗📁Vics Canvas will attempt to become the oldest Grand National winner since 1853 when he lines up for the famous race in April as a 14-year-old, but he must do so without a prep-run because of a badly timed setback. The Irish raider, a heroic third in last year’s race after all but falling at Becher’s Brook on the first circuit, was supposed to make his reappearance in December but sustained a minor leg injury. “You’ll see him in the National, but he won’t get a run before then,” revealed Dermot McLoughlin, his County Meath-based trainer, who had planned to race the horse in Britain at the end of last year, either in the Becher Chase or a veterans race at Kelso. “He got a little knock on his joint, there was a little bit of a crack there.

🔗📁“We only found out about it a week before he was going to run. He seems fine now and he’s back on the go again.” The career of Vics Canvas has been a slow-burning affair, partly because of the stomach ulcers that plagued him as a youngster. He was already seven by the time he achieved his first success under rules, in McLoughlin’s first season with a licence, and even now has had just 11 races over fences, his sole success coming in the Cork Grand National of 2014. It was hardly surprising that he was allowed to start at 100-1 at Aintree last spring but he proved those odds to be wildly wrong with a huge effort and was in front halfway up the run-in. McLoughlin was left to wonder what might have been, because the gelding, eventually beaten by 14 lengths, lost at least that much ground with his early stumble on the landing side of Becher’s.

🔗📁“There’s two things to say about that,” the trainer reflected. “He was very unlucky it happened to him but at the same time he was lucky to keep going and lucky he didn’t get hurt. He was down on his knees. “He has the heart of a lion, a lot of horses would have packed it in after that. He jumped really well the rest of the way.” The 42-year-old McLoughlin, who has a full yard of 35 animals at his base near Fairyhouse racecourse, seems to have decided pretty quickly that Vics Canvas should be kept going for another tilt at the National, despite his advancing years. “He still has the same enthusiasm about the game and he’s lightly raced. He’s in good nick and hopefully he stays right until then.”

🔗📁The betting market is again sceptical about the veteran’s prospects, as odds of 66-1 are available about him for the race on 8 April. No 14-year-old has ever won the National and the only older horse to win it was Peter Simple at the age of 15 in 1853, when the field of 21 runners was half as many as will line up this year. Peter Simple had already won the race as an 11-year-old. But, as McLoughlin points out, Vics Canvas is already something of a trends-buster. When he ran third last year, he became the first horse as old as 13 to be placed in the Grand National since 1969.

🔗📁Along with all other Grand National contenders, Vics Canvas will have to be passed fit to take part by British Horseracing Authority vets, who will inspect the runners at Aintree on the morning of the race. Before then, a BHA panel will consider the profiles of all those entered and may challenge the connections of any horses not thought suitable to take part in steeplechasing’s toughest test. Nico De Boinville is due to make his return to action with a single ride at Catterick on Friday. The 27-year-old jockey broke an arm in a fall at Cheltenham in mid-November but can now hope to be reunited with the exciting Altior in the Game Spirit at Newbury a week on Saturday.

🔗📁Sport | Horse Racing Martin Dwyer is the first to admit it is still surreal that he will once again find himself saddling up at Royal Ascot later on Tuesday. The festival will be awash with its usual pageantry in the build-up to the 45-year-old’s first ride of the week on board Palavecino in the Wolferton Stakes. But it is a far cry from the Liverpool council estate where he dreamt of becoming the next player to don Everton’s colours rather than be first past the winning post at the Berkshire racecourse. “The closest I go to riding was we played football and my mate’s sister kept a little pony on the side of the pitches,” he recalls.

🔗📁“I’d play football on the Saturday morning of the Grand National and watch the helicopters fly over to land at Aintree,” Dwyer said. But his aspiration was not then to ride winners, instead he added: “I used to say ‘one day I’d go in a helicopter’.” But thanks to his father’s passion for races and 10 pence accumulators at the local betting shop, he “got the bug for it”, and despite the unlikely upbringing not in keeping with much of the rest of the equine world, he got a chance as a 15-year-old apprentice with Ian Balding. There have been no shortage of big races in the intervening three decades: the Derby, Oaks and most recently this year’s QIPCO Champions Series Coronation Cup on board Pyledriver, making him only the third jockey in history to win all three big races at Epsom alongside Frankie Dettori and Ryan Moore.

🔗📁Eleven days before the opening afternoon at the Festival is mighty close to the season’s main event to give a potential Grade One horse his Cheltenham prep. Le Breuil looked every inch a Festival contender here on Friday, however, as he flew the obstacles with speed and accuracy on the way to a deeply impressive nine-length success, and Ben Pauling, his trainer, made it plain afterwards that the five-year-old is a match for anything in his stable. Since Pauling’s Festival entries include High Bridge and Willoughby Court, who are both priced at around 16-1 for Festival targets, Le Breuil is clearly a horse with a future. Whether it is an immediate future, however, remains to be seen.

🔗📁“The reason I left him in at Cheltenham was just in case he came out of this like a bull in a china shop, then we’ve got our options,” Pauling said. “I think he’s that calibre, but if we don’t go to Cheltenham, we can look towards Aintree. “I think this is as good as we’ve got, so hopefully all being well, tomorrow morning we’ll make a few plans. I’m pleased I left him in because it gives us options, but the only thing we’ll do is what’s in the best interests of the horse.” Le Breuil holds entries in both the Neptune and the Albert Bartlett Novice Hurdles, on 15 March and 17 March respectively, but the recent statistics are not promising. Over the last 10 years, 37 horses have lined up for a Grade One at the Festival less than a fortnight after their previous race. Not one has managed to win, and only one – in the Bumper – has even made the frame.

🔗📁Michael Scudamore has around 25 horses in his yard, which would have been a fair string when his late grandfather, also Michael, started training in the 1960s, but is a handful by modern standards. In the last 10 days, however, he has now sent out four winners from seven starters, including Kingswell Theatre in the Devon National and Mysteree in the Eider Chase, one of the highlights of Newcastle’s season over jumps. Most Celebrated, who was quoted at around 33-1 for the Triumph Hurdle before the race, set off as the 2-1 favourite, and looked a certain winner as Tom Scudamore, Michael’s brother, eased him into the lead after jumping the last. He found nothing in the closing stages, however, and offered no resistance as Dinsdale stayed on to win by one-and-a-quarter lengths. Dinsdale picked up a 5lb penalty in the process which could squeeze him in at the bottom of the weights for the Fred Winter on 15 March.

🔗📁Aintree has thrown a ring of steel around the famous Grand National course at the start of the three-day racing festival. In the wake of the terror attacks in Paris and Brussels , race-goers faced added security measures as they arrived at the course. All cars were checked inside and out, with drivers and passengers asked to leave their vehicles as the sweeps were completed. Engine compartments and boots were all thoroughly inspected. And security guards used military-style under-car mirrors to check for explosive devices. Metal detectors, body and bag searches were also in use. Punters arriving for Friday’s packed out Ladies Day on Merseyside have been warned to arrive early to avoid long queues at the entrances. Police say there have not been any direct threats to the race meeting. 🔗📁Grand National office sweepstakes 'could be illegal if you're working from home' A top law firm has warned that the traditional office sweepstake could land you in hot water with the Gambling Commission if anyone taking part is working from home The Grand National is one of the most popular events for an annual office sweepstake (Image: Getty Images) The Grand National is traditionally an event when even people who aren’t normally interested in horse racing are tempted to have a flutter but businesses could now be breaking the rules if they have staff working from home. ‌ But the shift towards people working from home as a result of the coronavirus pandemic could potentially land the organisers of office sweepstakes in trouble.

🔗📁‌ In pre-Covid times the office sweepstake was a regular annual fixture, with everyone from the boss to the office junior taking part. ‌ But now, leading law firm Poppleston Allen says businesses operating “hybrid working” with some or all of their employees currently working remotely, may risk falling foul of gambling licensing laws with the running of the sweepstake. Home workers are taking a bigger chance then they realise if they place a bet at 'the office' (Image: Getty Images) Richard Bradley, associate solicitor and gambling regulation expert at Poppleston Allen, said: “While formal gambling activity is heavily regulated by the Gambling Commission, there is an exception designed to allow the general public to have a bit of fun by taking part in what is officially called a work lottery.

🔗📁‌ “But what many people may not realise is that the rules are very clear in that you can only sell physical tickets and all players must work in the same office – contests running across different office locations of the same company are not allowed. “Therefore, if the pandemic has led to staff working from other offices or largely working from home, extra care needs to be taken when running a Grand National sweepstake. “Organisers, whether employers or employees, must make sure they do not sell any tickets via email or over the phone. Any staff member who wants to play must visit the office and buy a physical ticket. If these rules aren’t followed, organisers and players would technically be involved in illegal gambling.”

🔗📁There were times, such as the spring of 2003 when a 23-year-old Geraghty won the first of two awards for the top rider at Cheltenham, when he seemed to have no equals in producing a flawless ride when it mattered most. Geraghty’s five winners that year – doubles on Tuesday and Thursday, with Moscow Flyer’s first Champion Chase on the middle day - equalled the record for a three-day Festival. Just over three weeks later, he landed the Grand National on Monty’s Pass. Quick Guide Pinatubo bounces back with Prix Jean Prat win Show Pinatubo got back on the winning trail with a stylish victory in the Qatar Prix Jean Prat at Deauville. The 1-2 favourite, dropped to seven furlongs for this Group One race after two recent defeats, made his backers sweat before pulling away under William Buick. Charlie Appleby's stable star was crowned last season's champion two-year-old after an unbeaten six-race campaign, but came third in the 2,000 Guineas and lost to Palace Pier in the St James's Palace Stakes at Ascot. Pinatubo got back to form here despite getting stuck in a pocket for the first half of the race as he tracked fellow British raider Molatham.

🔗📁Once the chance came, Godolphin-owned colt quickly moved through the gears and won with something to spare. Aidan O'Brien's Lope Y Fernandez was a clear second, with Marco Botti's Malotru third. "It sounds strange, but I felt he lost nothing in defeat in the Guineas or at Ascot," Appleby said afterwards. "I came here today with plenty of confidence, to be honest. We knew dropping back to seven furlongs would be his bag, and while it was a bit of a rough race, when you're riding a horse like him everything just seems so easy." The Newmarket handler added that Pinatubo was unlikely to race in the upcoming Sussex Stakes at Goodwood. "We might be better giving him a little bit more time," Appleby said. "If we wanted to stretch him out to a mile again, the obvious race is the Prix du Moulin. If we wanted to stick at seven [furlongs] we could wait for the Prix de la Foret before taking him to Keeneland for the Breeders' Cup Mile." PA Media Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

🔗📁Geraghty, in fact, was more dependable than Walsh when he got on a Cheltenham Festival favourite, with a 48% strike-rate on clear favourites from 2003 onwards. Walsh’s strike-rate on clear favourites over the same period was 41%. But while Geraghty rode 39 market leaders in that time, Walsh was aboard 86. Geraghty had not been riding since jump racing resumed in Ireland last month and while the last mount of his exceptional career was pulled up at Uttoxeter on 14 March, his final ride at the Cheltenham Festival a day earlier was a winner (and favourite): Saint Roi, who landed a big gamble in the McManus colours in the County Hurdle.

🔗📁He also retires as a winner of all four of the Cheltenham Festival’s feature events, having landed two Gold Cups, four Champion Hurdles, a joint-record five Champion Chases and two Stayers’ Hurdles. Away from Cheltenham and in addition to his Grand National success, he took the King George at Kempton on Boxing Day in 2004 and 2005 on Kicking King, while Moscow Flyer’s defeat of the favourite Azertyuiop (and Walsh) in an epic Tingle Creek at Sandown in 2004 is another outstanding memory. There were, inevitably, some shocking injuries along the way, including a broken leg in a fall at Aintree in April 2019 which many thought might end his career there and then. Typically, he was not only back at Cheltenham four months ago, but in outstanding form with five winners, including Epatante’s Champion Hurdle, and being denied a third top-rider award at the Festival only on countback.

🔗📁Tom Scudamore, one of the most successful jump jockeys of all time, has retired with immediate effect, bringing to an end one of racing’s greatest riding dynasties. Scudamore broke the news to trainer David Pipe, for whom he has been stable jockey since 2007, on Thursday night. The 40-year-old made his decision after being unseated from Ya Know Yaseff at Leicester on Thursday. In a career that lasted a quarter of a century, Scudamore rode 1,511 winners, a tally that puts him 10th in the list of all-time jump jockeys. 🔗📁Jenny Pitman Extract Peter Darsebury rang me late and told me I had to go down to Lambourn first to appease Jenny Pitman who was naturally upset about Esha Ness “winning” a void race. She wanted recognition, not for her but for the horse and the connections. “You cannot concede anything at all.” said, Peter. “No prize money, no trophy, no winners rug and no name on the Roll of Honour boards.” A horrid situation for everyone but as Peter explained once you conceded anything you were accepting a “winner” and there wasn’t one. I arrived at Weathercock House at about 8.30 and was greeted by David Stait, Jenny’s husband. He told me Jenny had been crying lots and would be down in a while.

Mark Johnston reports that Great British Racing are mucking about with the birthdates of all racehorses, Hayley Turner uses Twitter to say she’s getting a jumps licence, ATR says two of their presenters have had their hair cut to look like Jedward and on and on … though, interestingly, the Racing Post hasn’t printed an April Fool story this year, possibly because so many racing stories are pretty hard to believe in any case. I quite liked the effort by Paul Nicholls through his Betfair blog, which suggested he was going to commandeer the horses trained by his former assistants, Dan Skelton and Harry Fry, in an effort to repel Willie Mullins’ assault on his title. Nicholls has such a reputation for competitiveness that quite a few people would believe him capable of such a thing, which is why he gets my respect for signing up to the joke.

🔗📁Anyway, it’s lucky 1 April wasn’t yesterday or you might have thought I was kidding about tipping Hurricane Volta, the horse with no form, at Wolverhampton. The nearest thing I can offer to a sexy outsider is Arquebusier (3.25), an 8-1 shot for a handicap chase at Fontwell. This six-year-old has done well since joining Emma Baker from Ireland, winning two handicap hurdles and running second at Towcester. The step up in class was too much for him at Sandown in early February but he’s had a good break and now goes over fences, a sphere in which he ran well on his only previous attempt in Ireland. There’s a chance he’ll get his own way in front and he’ll be handily treated if he can build on his hurdles form.

Meanwhile, and not coincidentally, the Champion Hurdle appears a bit short on star power, the final field of 12 being headed by Yanworth and Buveur D’Air. The trainers of those two, respectively Alan King and Nicky Henderson, walked the course together on Sunday morning. “It’s softer than I expected,” King said. “The Old Course [to be used on Tuesday and Wednesday], from the stands right to the top of the hill, I would put it nearly as soft. It’s a little bit quicker down the hill, good to soft there. The New Course would be good to soft, good down the back and a bit slower up the straight. So it’s got a lot of moisture in it.”

🔗📁Red Rum makes a special guest appearance (1977) Sports Personality has a habit of attracting some of the most famous sports stars on the planet – usually human, but not always. Red Rum was the toast of the nation in 1977 when he stormed to an amazing third Grand National triumph at Aintree, and it seemed only logical the BBC would want ‘Rummy’ to appear at its December bash. Red Rum was introduced by Frank Bough with the words ‘Welcome the maestro himself.’ Trainer Ginger McCain said his famous horse just enjoyed the big stage. ‘He’s been listening to the applause at the back, and he thinks it’s for him all the time,’ McCain said. His jockey, Tommy Stack, joined proceedings via a video link, and when Bough asked him to ‘give Red Rum a shout’, Stack amusingly said: ‘I don’t know what to say to him, he’s much more intelligent than I am.’

🔗📁The bankers working in London and the US exchanged emails to deliberately skew the US dollar Libor rate between 2005 and 2007, involving ‘eye-watering’ sums of money to rake in profits on top of their hefty bonuses. James Hines, QC, prosecuting, compared their scam to cheating at roulette by getting a croupier to place the ball where you bet or asking a Grand National jockey to slow down in a race. He said the operation was like ‘very large scale executive gambling’. Jay Merchant, left, and Alex Pabon, right, who were working for the bank in New York, would email rate requests to Mathew in London.

🔗📁Even Jonbon, Wednesday’s hot favourite, cannot afford to take a liberty. Nicky Henderson’s pride and joy has been beaten only three times in 20 career starts – a phenomenal record – but his losses (from five visits) have all come at Cheltenham. One was a shocker, a 1-4 defeat at the start of last year, due entirely to him making a Horlicks of jumping one fence. In fairness, the other two blemishes on his otherwise perfect CV were beatings by the remarkable Constitution Hill over hurdles and by a peak-form El Fabiolo in the 2023 Arkle Trophy. Jonbon, currently on a roll of five successive wins, including four Grade Ones, is at his peak now. He’s popular with the public and they’ll be keeping fingers crossed that he sails over every one of the 13 fences without mishap before roaring him home for a first Festival triumph.

🔗📁He previously fractured his jaw in six places, punctured his lungs, broke ‘just about every rib’ and suffered six concussions. Maxwell rode all the horses he owned and memorably finished sixth in the 2024 Grand National on 40-1 Ain’t That A Shame. That landed the hugely successful property developer a cheque for £30,000 and showed he truly could cut it with the pros. Maxwell was going so well at one point on the Henry de Bromhead-trained runner that he thought he was going to win the world’s most famous race. But, cruelly, it was a fall last season, also at Aintree in the famous Foxhunters race, that proved the final blow.

Maxwell rode the Gary & Josh Moore-trained gelding to fifth in this year’s Champion Bumper. 🔗📁Bookies have quickly taken notice too. With Maxwell no longer the rider they somewhat cynically cut his odds to 25-1 from 33s for this season’s Supreme Novices’ Hurdle. But that rather sums up the love-hate relationship punters had with larger-than-life Maxwell. His horses were always priced bigger than they should have been on account of him riding. And for all he was a champion amateur with a Grade 3 victory in France, sometimes it was painfully obvious why he had to play second fiddle to the pros. Maxwell himself was aware of it, telling the Telegraph: “About ten years ago, for a present, the guys in the office blew up and framed a Tweet under ‘hashtag shockingride’, saying that the tweeter wished ‘David Maxwell would stop riding his own horses’.

🔗📁It is a while ago since trainer Kim Bailey won the Champion Hurdle, Gold Cup and Grand National. Since those halcyon days his fortunes have meet with triumph and almost disaster. His move to Northamptonshire resulted in him enduring a career low with six winners in 2005 and the same number 12 months later. But a subsequent move to the Cotswolds was the catalyst to a welcome resurgence in fortunes and his runners are always to be respected. Bailey has started this season off in flying form, but it is his runners in the month of October that make the most appealing reading as he has had now fewer than six winners from only 12 runners.

🔗📁His stablemate Imperial Aura (1.55) is another trying a new discipline for the first time when he runs in the opening 2m3f novices’ hurdle at Carlisle. The son of Kalanisi only had two runs last season, both in bumpers, but it was the manner of his most recent effort when readily pulling away in the closing stages at Ludlow that marked him out as an interesting horse for the future. Bailey’s horses usually know their jobs when they go jumping so it can be taken as read that the selection will be ready to go. For my next best we have to wait until the last race of the day, the 1m5f novice stakes at Chelmsford. The horse in question is Keltie (8.45) who impressed me as much as any maiden I have seen for a while when easily winning at Kempton last time. The daughter of Giant’s Causeway has clearly not been straightforward as she didn’t make her debut until the middle of September, missing her juvenile season completely and most of the current one. But after a very pleasing fourth at Chelmsford she showed she had learnt from the experience as once she found her stride she flew up the Kempton straight and won going away with something in hand.

The Dubai World Cup meeting will go ahead on March 28 'without paid hospitality spectators'.

🔗📁Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, 5-6 October, Longchamp The chance to once again see Enable, the outstanding thoroughbred on these shores, will be of huge interest to all racing aficionados. Her date with destiny is the first Sunday in October at Longchamp when she will attempt to become the first triple winner of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe. Frankie Dettori on board is very much an added bonus. Elsewhere in 2019, the vintage two-year-old crop consisting of Too Darn Hot, Ten Sovereigns, Calyx and Quorto are set to clash in the 2,000 Guineas in May, while over jumps Cheltenham will take centre stage in March and the Grand National in April.

🔗📁The BBC has warned stars not to promote brands - after a radio presenter broke rules when covering last month's Grand National. Gina Bryce, a horse racing presenter on Radio 5 Live, promoted Bee Smith Millinery and Jane Lewis Atelier in a tweet about the corporation's coverage of the famous race, The Times reports. The star wrote: 'Grand National Day. Join me and the amazing @bbc5live team from 12pm today for all the buildup' on Twitter and tagged the two brands. 🔗📁The corporation has now reissued guidance on the matter. BBC's editorial guidelines state: 'No on-air talent should promote products, goods, services or clothing they use on air.' The corporation said that a complaint which had been made had merit, saying: 'With regards to a tweet posted by Gina on the day, tagging the brands she was wearing, while also tagging the BBC 5 Live page and discussing her work, we do agree that this would go beyond the BBC's usual expectations.' The complaint submitted by Alex May also focussed on Bryce's work with Paddy Power but she was ruled to not have broken rules in that partnership.

🔗📁The Irish raider has plenty of strong form over staying trips, including a win on testing ground over 3m4f at Punchestown last year. She ran well for a long way when fancied for the Grand National in April, still in contention when she was badly hampered six fences from home. She completed and finished 12th, but bettered that performance on her next start when winning a big pot in France. The seven-year-old mare is reported to be ‘bigger and stronger’ than when she ran a cracking fifth in this race in 2016. She is on a good mark, will have come on plenty for her comeback run and has no concerns about ground on trip. This has been her target for a while.

🔗📁It is one of the biggest races of the National Hunt season. Where is the King George VI Chase run? The race is run at Kempton Park racecourse, which is located in Sunbury, Surrey. When is the King George VI Chase run? The King George will be run at 3.05pm on Boxing Day (Wednesday, December 26). Where can I watch the King George VI Chase The race will be broadcast live on both ITV1 and Racing TV. Racing TV is a subscription channel and is on Sky channel 426, Virgin channel 536, and UPC in Ireland on channel 411. ITV1 can be found on Sky channel 103 and Virgin channel 103.

The Japan Racing Association revealed that 'government-sanctioned races' will go ahead behind closed doors. Racing in Ireland attempted to take place behind closed doors starting on March 29 - but that decision was changed after government cancelled all sporting events. The Dubai World Cup meeting will go ahead on March 28 'without paid hospitality spectators'.

🔗📁‌ 2. Decide whether you want to bet to win (meaning the horse has to finish first) or each-way (meaning the horse must finish in first four, in the case of the Grand National). An each-way bet is twice the cost, as the stake goes on the horse both to win, and to be placed. ‌ 3. On to the slip, write down the name of your big-race selection(s), the time of the race and the course. e.g. £5 win Teaforthree 4.15 Aintree, or, £5 each-way Teaforthree 4.15 Aintree (with the total stake for the latter coming to £10). Most bookmakers will accept it if you simply put, for example, £5 win Teaforthree, Grand National.

🔗📁4. Next you should go to the counter to pay for your bet. The odds you get will be the official starting price, declared after the race. However, if you wish, you can choose to back the horse at the price currently offered by the bookmaker in the shop, by telling the assistant you wish to “take the price”. Doing so guarantees you the specific odds that are on offer at the time, so even if the horse’s price drops later on, you will still collect at the larger price. ‌ 5. The assistant will hand you back a copy of the betting slip which you should retain, to allow you to collect your winnings.

🔗📁‌ The advent of betting exchanges, along with bookmaker telephone and internet accounts, allows even a recluse to enjoy the thrill of a punt. You can then click on to the website of the bookmaker who offers the best odds about your fancy, and by filling in an on-line form, which will include card details, you can place your bet and join in the thrill of the marathon contest.
